content: An epizootic refers to a sharp increase in the incidence rate of a disease within an animal population. The term epidemic is used in a similar context when referring to human populations. High population density is a significant factor contributing to the occurrence of epizootics. For example, aquaculture is an industry that is sometimes heavily affected by disease outbreaks due to the large number of fish confined to small areas. The definition of an epizootic can be subjective and depends, in part, on what is considered expected or normal. An epizootic can manifest in different ways: (a) it may be localized to a specific area, which is referred to as an outbreak, (b) it may occur more generally across a broader region, which is termed an epizootic, or (c) it may be widespread across multiple regions or continents, which is classified as a panzootic. Because the classification is based on what is considered expected, even a few cases of a very rare disease, such as a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy (TSE) outbreak in a cervid population, might be labeled as an epizootic. Conversely, a large number of cases of a common disease, such as lymphocystis in esocid fish, would not typically be classified as an epizootic. Diseases that occur at a constant but relatively high rate within a population are referred to as enzootic. An example of an enzootic disease would be the influenza virus in certain bird populations or, at a lower incidence, the Type IVb strain of viral hemorrhagic septicemia (VHS) in some Atlantic fish populations. In contrast, an example of an epizootic event would be the 1990 outbreak of Newcastle disease virus in double-crested cormorant colonies around the Great Lakes, which resulted in the death of approximately 10,000 birds. On September 14, 2007, an outbreak of epizootic ulcerative syndrome (EUS), a mysterious and severe disease, caused the death of hundreds of fish covered in sores in the Zambezi River in Zambia. In response, Zambia's Agriculture Minister, Ben Kapita, requested experts to investigate the outbreak to determine its cause and assess whether the disease could be transmitted to humans.
